name: gitcode
short: GitCode CLI - Command line tool for GitCode
long:
gitcode is a command line tool for GitCode.

It provides convenient access to GitCode features including:
  - Authentication management (auth login, auth status)
  - Repository operations (repo clone, repo create)
  - Issue management (issue create, issue list)
  - Pull Request management (pr create, pr review)

subcommands.name: actions
subcommands.long:
Work with GitCode Actions: inspect pipeline runs and workflow jobs,
or enable and disable repository Actions.

Changing repository Actions permissions is a dangerous operation and
requires confirmation unless --yes is provided.
subcommands.example:
# List recent pipeline runs
$ gitcode actions run list -R owner/repo

# Filter runs by status
$ gitcode actions run list -R owner/repo --status FAILED

# Output runs as JSON
$ gitcode actions run list -R owner/repo --json

# List jobs of a pipeline run
$ gitcode actions job list <run-id> -R owner/repo

subcommands.name: artifact
subcommands.long: Inspect workflow run artifacts for a repository.
subcommands.example:
# List repository artifacts
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo

# View an artifact detail
$ gitcode actions artifact view <artifact-id> -R owner/repo

# Download an artifact
$ gitcode actions artifact download <artifact-id> -R owner/repo --output artifact.zip

# Delete an artifact
$ gitcode actions artifact delete <artifact-id> -R owner/repo --yes

subcommands.name: delete
subcommands.long:
Delete a workflow artifact from a GitCode repository.

This is a destructive operation. By default it asks for confirmation
(type the artifact id to confirm). In non-interactive mode, --yes is
required to skip confirmation. Use --dry-run to preview without deleting.
subcommands.example:
# Delete an artifact (interactive)
$ gitcode actions artifact delete <artifact-id> -R owner/repo

# Non-interactive (requires --yes)
$ gitcode actions artifact delete <artifact-id> -R owner/repo --yes

# Preview the deletion
$ gitcode actions artifact delete <artifact-id> -R owner/repo --dry-run

# JSON output
$ gitcode actions artifact delete <artifact-id> -R owner/repo --yes --json

subcommands.name: download
subcommands.long:
Download a workflow artifact as a ZIP archive.

The artifact id is the `id` returned by `gc actions artifact list`.
The endpoint returns a ZIP archive (binary); use --output to save it,
or redirect stdout (e.g. > artifact.zip). On an interactive terminal
without --output it refuses to dump the binary archive.
subcommands.example:
# Save artifact to a file
$ gitcode actions artifact download <artifact-id> -R owner/repo --output artifact.zip

# Stream to a file via redirect
$ gitcode actions artifact download <artifact-id> -R owner/repo > artifact.zip

flags.name: output
flags.usage: Write artifact ZIP to FILE (default: stdout)

subcommands.name: list
subcommands.long:
List workflow run artifacts for a GitCode repository.

Filters are applied server-side via the Actions v8 API. Use --json for
machine-readable output.
subcommands.example:
# List repository artifacts
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo

# List artifacts of a specific run
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo --run <run-id>

# Filter by name (fuzzy)
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo --name build

# Sort by creation time
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo --sort created --direction desc

# Fetch all pages
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo --paginate --per-page 100

# Render as a table
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo --format table

# Output as JSON
$ gitcode actions artifact list -R owner/repo --json

subcommands.name: list
subcommands.short: List workflow jobs of a pipeline run
subcommands.long:
List the workflow jobs of a single pipeline run.

The run id is the workflow_run_id returned by `gc actions run list`.
Use --json for machine-readable output.
subcommands.example:
# List jobs of a pipeline run
$ gitcode actions job list <run-id> -R owner/repo

# Render as a table

subcommands.name: log
subcommands.long:
Download the log of a single workflow job.

Both the run id (workflow_run_id from `gc actions run list`) and the
job id (from `gc actions job list`) are required, matching the API
path /actions/runs/{run_id}/jobs/{job_id}/download_log. The endpoint
returns a ZIP archive of the job's step logs (binary, not plain text),
so prefer --output to save and unzip; writing to stdout streams the raw
archive bytes (use a redirect, e.g. > job-log.zip).
subcommands.example:
# Save the job log archive and unzip it
$ gitcode actions job log <run-id> <job-id> -R owner/repo --output job-log.zip
$ unzip job-log.zip

# Stream the raw archive to a file via redirect
$ gitcode actions job log <run-id> <job-id> -R owner/repo > job-log.zip

subcommands.name: view
subcommands.long:

Both the run id (workflow_run_id from `gc actions run list`) and the
job id (from `gc actions job list`) are required, matching the API
path /actions/runs/{run_id}/jobs/{job_id}. Use --json for a faithful,
machine-readable copy of the API response.
subcommands.example:
# View a workflow job
$ gitcode actions job view <run-id> <job-id> -R owner/repo

# Faithful JSON output (all API fields preserved)
$ gitcode actions job view <run-id> <job-id> -R owner/repo --json

subcommands.name: plugin
subcommands.long:
Query the official GitCode Actions plugin directory and usage docs.

Plugins are published by GitCode and provide reusable workflow steps.
Use the list subcommand to discover available plugins and the view
subcommand to inspect a plugin's versions and README.
subcommands.example:
# List available plugins for a repository
$ gitcode actions plugin list -R owner/repo

# View a plugin's README and versions
$ gitcode actions plugin view checkout -R owner/repo

# Output as JSON
$ gitcode actions plugin list -R owner/repo --json

subcommands.name: list
subcommands.long:
List official GitCode Actions plugins available for a repository.

By default all pages are fetched automatically. Use --limit,
--page, or --per-page to control pagination.
subcommands.example:

$ gitcode actions plugin list -R owner/repo

# Fetch a single page
$ gitcode actions plugin list -R owner/repo --page 1 --per-page 20

# Output as JSON
$ gitcode actions plugin list -R owner/repo --json

# Write output to a file (avoids shell encoding issues)
$ gitcode actions plugin list -R owner/repo --json --files plugins.json

subcommands.name: rerun
subcommands.short: Rerun all jobs of a pipeline run
subcommands.long:
Rerun all jobs of a pipeline (workflow) run.

The run id is the workflow_run_id returned by `gc actions run list`.
Only runs in a complete status can be rerun; rerunning a run that is
still RUNNING fails with a conflict error. Use --json for a
machine-readable result.

Non-interactive mode: Requires --yes to skip confirmation.
subcommands.example:
# Rerun a pipeline run
$ gitcode actions run rerun <run-id> -R owner/repo

# Skip confirmation (for scripts)
$ gitcode actions run rerun <run-id> -R owner/repo --yes

# JSON output
$ gitcode actions run rerun <run-id> -R owner/repo --yes --json

subcommands.name: retry
subcommands.short: Retry failed or canceled jobs of a pipeline run
subcommands.long:
Retry selected jobs of a pipeline (workflow) run without rerunning the
whole run. Only runs in a failed or canceled status can be retried.

The run id is the workflow_run_id returned by `gc actions run list`;
job ids are the job_run_id values returned by `gc actions job list <run-id>`.

Exactly one of --job or --failed is required. Job ids are validated
against the target run before the request is sent, because the server
silently accepts job ids belonging to other runs.

Non-interactive mode: Requires --yes to skip confirmation.
subcommands.example:
# Retry specific jobs (repeatable)
$ gitcode actions run retry <run-id> --job <job-id> --job <job-id-2> -R owner/repo

# Retry all failed/canceled jobs
$ gitcode actions run retry <run-id> --failed -R owner/repo

# Skip confirmation (for scripts)
$ gitcode actions run retry <run-id> --failed --yes -R owner/repo

# JSON output
$ gitcode actions run retry <run-id> --failed --yes --json

flags.name: failed
flags.usage: Retry all failed/canceled jobs of the run

subcommands.long:

The run id is the workflow_run_id returned by `gc actions run list`.
The API is idempotent: stopping a run that has already finished still

Non-interactive mode: Requires --yes to skip confirmation.
subcommands.example:

$ gitcode actions run stop <run-id> -R owner/repo

# Skip confirmation (for scripts)
$ gitcode actions run stop <run-id> -R owner/repo --yes

# JSON output
$ gitcode actions run stop <run-id> -R owner/repo --yes --json

subcommands.name: watch
subcommands.short: Watch a pipeline run until completion
subcommands.long:
Watch a pipeline run, refreshing its status at regular intervals until
the run reaches a terminal state (COMPLETED, FAILED, CANCELED,
IGNORED, PAUSED, or SUSPEND).

In a TTY, the screen is refreshed on each poll. In a non-TTY
environment (e.g. piped output or --no-interactive), a single
snapshot is printed and the command exits immediately; pass
--wait to keep polling in non-TTY mode until the run reaches a
terminal state (--exit-status then works as in a TTY).

Use --exit-status to exit with a non-zero code when the run fails.
subcommands.example:
# Watch a run until it finishes
$ gitcode actions run watch <run-id> -R owner/repo

# Watch with a 10-second interval
$ gitcode actions run watch <run-id> -R owner/repo --interval 10

# Compact mode (only failed steps)
$ gitcode actions run watch <run-id> -R owner/repo --compact

# Exit non-zero on failure (for CI scripts)
$ gitcode actions run watch <run-id> -R owner/repo --exit-status

# Wait for completion from a script (non-interactive)
$ gitcode actions run watch <run-id> -R owner/repo --wait --exit-status

flags.name: exit-status
flags.usage: Exit with non-zero status if run failed

flags.name: wait
flags.usage: In non-interactive mode, keep polling until the run reaches a terminal state

subcommands.name: setting
subcommands.long:
Enable or disable GitCode Actions for one repository or for every
repository in an organization. Use -R owner/repo for one repository,
or --org <name> for all repositories in an organization. When neither
is given, the repository is inferred from the current git repository,
like the rest of the actions command family.

The command reads each repository's current Actions permission first,
then changes only action_enabled and preserves the other permission
fields. This is a dangerous operation: it asks you to type
"<action> Actions for <target>" (for example,
"enable Actions for owner/repo") to confirm, or use --yes in a
non-interactive environment. When no repository needs a change, the
command reports the result without asking for confirmation.
Before confirmation, the command warns that it uses a Web API endpoint
not documented in the official GitCode API reference.

The Actions settings endpoint requires a GitCode web-session JWT; a
classic personal access token cannot be used for this request. The
command explains how to obtain it from a signed-in GitCode browser
session. Interactive input is hidden and held in memory only for this
command. In non-interactive environments, pipe it via --with-token
and never place a token literal on the command line.
subcommands.example:
# Enable Actions for one repository
$ gitcode actions setting enable -R owner/repo

# Enable Actions for the current repository
$ gitcode actions setting enable

# Disable Actions for one repository without an interactive prompt
$ gitcode actions setting disable -R owner/repo --yes

# Enable Actions for every repository in an organization
$ gitcode actions setting enable --org my-org

# Enable all repositories and return structured output
$ gitcode actions setting enable --org my-org --yes --json

# Non-interactive: pipe the web session JWT. Never echo or cat a
# token literal (it leaks to shell history or disk); pipe it from
# a secret manager instead.
$ <print-token-from-secret-manager> | gitcode actions setting disable -R owner/repo --with-token --yes

flags.name: org
flags.usage: Organization name; batch every repository in it (mutually exclusive with -R)

flags.name: repo
flags.usage: Repository (owner/repo, defaults to the current repository)

flags.name: with-token
flags.usage: Read the gitcode.com web session JWT from standard input

not start with /api/, the CLI prefixes /api/v5 automatically.

$ gitcode api 'repos/owner/repo/commits?path=src/main.go&sha=main'

# Send a PATCH request with a JSON body
$ gitcode api repos/owner/repo/pulls/123 --method PATCH --input body.json

# Inspect response headers (ETag, rate limit) and filter output
$ gitcode api repos/owner/repo --include
$ gitcode api user --jq .login

# Fetch every page of an issue list, merged into one array
$ gitcode api 'repos/owner/repo/issues?state=all&per_page=100' --paginate --slurp

subcommands.name: auth
subcommands.long:
Authenticate with a GitCode account.

Environment variables:
  GC_CONFIG_DIR  Read and write configuration (including the
      login state) from this directory instead of the default
      ~/.config/gc. Point it at a separate directory to keep an
      isolated login, e.g. for a second account on one machine:
      an empty directory is "not logged in" and never falls
      back to the default directory.

subcommands.name: git-credential
subcommands.short: Provide stored GitCode credentials to git (helper protocol)
subcommands.long:
Implement the git credential helper protocol so that git operations
over HTTPS against GitCode use the credentials of the account logged
in via gc auth login.

git invokes this command with an operation argument (get, store or
erase) and a key=value request on stdin. Only "get" is meaningful:
when the request host matches the logged-in account, the username and
the access token are written to stdout in the credential protocol
format. store and erase are accepted as no-ops because gc does not
cache credentials beyond the login state.

When no credentials match, the command exits silently with a non-zero
status so git can try the next credential helper. Use gc auth status
to inspect the login state.

Credentials are served only from the account stored in the active
configuration directory: GC_CONFIG_DIR isolates the configuration
(useful for multiple accounts on one machine), while the
GC_TOKEN/GITCODE_TOKEN environment overrides intentionally do not
apply, so the helper's answer is fully determined by the login state
of the selected configuration directory. A GC_CONFIG_DIR that is set
to an empty value is treated as no configuration rather than falling
back to the default directory.
subcommands.example:
# Inspect what git would receive for the logged-in account
# (the password line is the access token; do not paste it into
# logs, screenshots, scripts, or AI agent contexts)
$ printf 'protocol=https\nhost=gitcode.com\n\n' | gitcode auth git-credential

# Configure git to use gc as a credential helper
$ gitcode auth setup-git

subcommands.name: login
subcommands.short: Log in to a GitCode account
subcommands.long:
Authenticate with a GitCode account.

By default, gc prompts for a token in an interactive terminal.
In non-interactive environments, use --with-token to read the token
from standard input.

Never place a token literal on the command line: it leaks to shell
history and process lists, and never store a token in a plaintext
file. Prefer interactive login, --web, or the GC_TOKEN environment
variable (injected from your platform's secrets); when using
--with-token, pipe from a secret manager.
subcommands.example:
# Start interactive login (recommended; use a private, unrecorded terminal)
$ gitcode auth login

# Login via browser device flow
$ gitcode auth login --web

# Login to a specific host
$ gitcode auth login --hostname gitcode.com

# Non-interactive (CI): inject the token via the GC_TOKEN environment
# variable from your platform's secrets; gc authenticates automatically,
# no login command needed.
#   $ export GC_TOKEN="$GC_TOKEN_FROM_SECRETS"

# Read a token from stdin with --with-token. Never echo/cat a token
# literal (it leaks to shell history or disk); pipe from a secret
# manager instead.
$ <print-token-from-secret-manager> | gitcode auth login --with-token

subcommands.name: logout

subcommands.long:

Hostnames are normalized and validated before logout.

The command prints current-session cleanup guidance on stderr.

$ gitcode auth logout

# Logout from a specific hostname
$ gitcode auth logout --hostname gitcode.com

subcommands.name: setup-git
subcommands.short: Configure git to use gc as a credential helper
subcommands.long:
Configure git to use gc as a credential helper so that git
operations against GitCode automatically carry authentication.

The credential helper entry is appended for the host without
overwriting existing credential helper configuration. Re-running
the command is safe: duplicate entries are skipped.

This is a client-side command: it does not call the GitCode API
and does not read or print tokens.

The configured helper points to the gc auth git-credential
subcommand, which fills the username and token of the account
logged in via gc auth login for HTTPS git operations.
subcommands.example:
# Configure the credential helper for the default host
$ gitcode auth setup-git

# Configure for a specific hostname
$ gitcode auth setup-git --hostname gitcode.com

subcommands.name: status
subcommands.long:
View information about your authentication status.

When no hostname is specified, checks for token from:
1. GC_TOKEN environment variable
2. GITCODE_TOKEN environment variable
3. Stored credentials from local config (~/.config/gc/auth.json)

gitcode.com
  ✓ Logged in as username (GC_TOKEN)
  ✓ Git operations protocol: https

# Output as JSON
$ gitcode auth status --json

subcommands.name: token
subcommands.long:
Print the authentication token for the current session.

The token is printed to stdout for use in scripts or piping.
For safety, this command requires an interactive confirmation.
If no token is found, returns an error.

gc_xxxxxxxxxxxx

# Use token in a script
$ TOKEN=$(gc auth token)

# Specify hostname
$ gitcode auth token --hostname gitcode.com

subcommands.name: browse

subcommands.long:

subcommands.long:

"npx @larksuite/cli@latest install". After install, run

subcommands.name: send
subcommands.short: Send a message to a Feishu/Lark chat or direct message
subcommands.long:
Send a message to a Feishu/Lark group, chat, or direct message by
delegating to "lark-cli im +messages-send".

Target resolution (--chat-id / --user-id / --to-self are mutually
exclusive; if none is given, the default chat from
"gc lark config set --default-chat" or GC_LARK_DEFAULT_CHAT_ID is
used):
  --chat-id oc_xxx   send to a group/chat
  --user-id ou_xxx   send a direct message to a person
  --to-self          send a direct message to the current lark-cli
                     user (resolves their open_id from "lark-cli auth
                     status"); defaults to the bot identity, which is
                     the common "notify myself" pattern that needs no
                     group membership.

Feishu OAuth credentials stay in lark-cli's OS keychain and are never
seen by gc. Message text (from --text, --markdown, or --body-file) is
scanned for the current GC_TOKEN/GITCODE_TOKEN value before sending.
subcommands.example:
# Notify yourself (bot -> you, no group needed)
$ gitcode lark send --to-self --text "deploy done"

# Send plain text to a specific group
$ gitcode lark send --chat-id oc_xxx --text "deploy done"

# Send a direct message to a person by open_id
$ gitcode lark send --user-id ou_xxx --as bot --text "hi"

# Use the configured default group
$ gitcode lark config set --default-chat oc_xxx
$ gitcode lark send --text "build green"

# Send markdown
$ gitcode lark send --chat-id oc_xxx --markdown "## Release\n- v1.2.3 shipped"

# Pipe a notification body from stdin
$ echo "ci passed" | gitcode lark send --to-self --body-file -

# Preview the lark-cli call without sending
$ gitcode lark send --to-self --text "hi" --dry-run

subcommands.name: review
subcommands.long:
Review a pull request in a GitCode repository.

You can approve, request changes, or comment on a PR.

Since GitCode's API does not natively support "request changes",
--request posts a comment with a [REQUEST CHANGES] prefix to signal
that changes are needed before the PR can be approved.

Note: --approve requires GitCode's "approval permission", which is
separate from the "merge permission" used by 'gc pr merge'. Users
with merge permission cannot approve PRs without explicit approval
permission granted by the repository administrators. If you receive
a 403 Forbidden error, use --comment to leave review feedback instead.
subcommands.example:
# Approve a PR
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --approve

# Comment on a PR
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --comment "Looks good to me"

# Comment from a file
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --comment-file review-notes.md

# Comment from stdin
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --comment-file -

# Approve a PR and leave a comment
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --approve --comment "LGTM"

# Approve a PR with comment from file
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --approve --comment-file self-check.md

# Request changes on a PR
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --request

# Request changes with a comment
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --request --comment "Please fix the error handling"

# Force approve a PR (admin only)
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --approve --force

# Output as JSON
$ gitcode pr review 123 -R owner/repo --approve --json

subcommands.short: View review states on a pull request
subcommands.long:

(with their accept_status), testers, and assignees.

The v5 API has no dedicated reviews list endpoint; these states
are embedded in the PR detail response. accept_status values:
true (approved), reject (rejected), optional (pending).
Per-reviewer timestamps are not provided by the endpoint.
subcommands.example:
# View review states on a PR
$ gitcode pr reviews 123 -R owner/repo

# Machine-readable output
$ gitcode pr reviews 123 -R owner/repo --json

subcommands.name: sync
subcommands.short: Sync a PR from one repository to another
subcommands.long:
Sync (cherry-pick) a pull request from one repository to another repository.

This command fetches the commits from the source PR, cherry-picks them into
a new branch in the target repository, and creates a new pull request.

The source PR can be specified as:
- owner/repo#number (e.g., gitcode-cli/cli#123)
- Full URL (e.g., https://gitcode.com/gitcode-cli/cli/merge_requests/123)

Git repository transfer uses SSH. Ensure an SSH key with access to git@gitcode.com is configured.

	Non-interactive mode: Requires --yes to skip confirmation.
subcommands.example:
# Sync PR #123 from source repo to target repo
$ gitcode pr sync --source-pr owner/source-repo#123 --target-repo owner/target-repo

# Specify target branch
$ gitcode pr sync --source-pr owner/source-repo#123 \
	--target-repo owner/target-repo \
	--base release/v1.0

# Custom title and body
$ gitcode pr sync --source-pr owner/source-repo#123 \
	--target-repo owner/target-repo \
	--title "[sync] Fix login bug" \
	--body "Synced from owner/source-repo#123"

# Create as draft
$ gitcode pr sync --source-pr owner/source-repo#123 \
	--target-repo owner/target-repo \
	--draft

# JSON output
$ gitcode pr sync --source-pr owner/source-repo#123 \
	--target-repo owner/target-repo \
	--json

subcommands.short: Work with pre-commit configuration and hooks
subcommands.long:
Detect and verify pre-commit configuration and the local pre-commit
environment before committing code.
subcommands.example:
# Verify the environment is ready
$ gitcode precommit check

# Verify and run the hooks
$ gitcode precommit check --run

subcommands.name: check
subcommands.short: Check pre-commit configuration before committing or pushing
subcommands.long:
Check whether the current repository configures pre-commit and whether the
local environment is ready before committing or pushing code.

The command:
  1. Detects a .pre-commit-config.yaml (or .yml) in the repository root.
  2. Verifies the pre-commit tool is installed.
  3. Verifies the git pre-commit and pre-push hooks are initialized.
  4. Optionally runs both hook stages with --run.

When something is missing it auto-installs/initializes in an interactive
terminal. In a non-interactive (non-TTY) environment, pass --yes to allow
environment changes, or --no-install to only diagnose. Cross-platform
(Windows, Linux x86/arm, macOS).
subcommands.example:
# Verify the environment is ready
$ gitcode precommit check

# Verify and actually run the hooks
$ gitcode precommit check --run

# Only diagnose, never modify the environment
$ gitcode precommit check --no-install

# Machine-readable output
$ gitcode precommit check --json

from the git remote. Pass an explicit <owner>/<repo> to
override. Use --view to display the current default, --unset
to clear it.
subcommands.example:
# Set default to current git remote's repository
$ gitcode repo set-default

# Set an explicit default
$ gitcode repo set-default owner/repo

# View the current default
$ gitcode repo set-default --view

# Clear the default
$ gitcode repo set-default --unset

subcommands.name: sync
subcommands.short: Sync a local directory into another repository and create a PR
subcommands.long:
Sync a directory from the current local repository into a target repository path.

The command clones the target repository into a temporary directory, copies the
source directory contents into the requested target directory, commits the change,
pushes a sync branch, and creates a pull request.

Git repository transfer uses SSH. Ensure an SSH key with access to git@gitcode.com is configured.

	Non-interactive mode: Requires --yes to skip confirmation.
subcommands.example:
# Sync local docs/api into another repo's sync/api directory
$ gitcode repo sync \
  --target-repo infra-test/target-repo \
  --source-dir docs/api \
  --target-dir sync/api

# Override base branch and PR title
$ gitcode repo sync \
  --target-repo infra-test/target-repo \
  --source-dir pkg/contracts \
  --target-dir mirror/contracts \
  --base main \
  --title "sync: update contracts"

# Output as JSON
$ gitcode repo sync --target-repo owner/repo --source-dir src --target-dir dst --json

subcommands.name: update
subcommands.short: Check for or apply an installation-channel update
subcommands.long:
Update GitCode CLI through the channel that owns the current installation.

Global npm wrappers update the installed npm coordinate (atomgit-cli,
@atomgit-cli/cli, or @gitcode-cli/cli) directly. npm-bootstrap installs run
a foreground update check first: when a newer stable version exists, the
atomic replacement is scheduled after the current process exits; otherwise
the current version is reported and nothing is scheduled. Other package
managers remain user-controlled and are never invoked or removed implicitly.
